caption:
ln + vpype — turning 3D scenes into lines for drawing.

① Build a 3D scene → ② remove hidden lines → ③ export vector paths → ④ arrange the drawing order.

ln removes lines hidden by the geometry. vpype joins and reorders the paths for pen plotting.

These scenes use ln's original examples with added camera motion. In this example, vpype linemerge + linesort reduced pen-up travel by 86% (105,271 → 14,926 px). This measures distance, not the time of a real pen plotter.

transcript: Today's open source project is LN, the 3D lineart engine. These scenes are 3D, but the output isn't pixels, it's lines. It's by Michael Fogelman, written in Go. He made it so he could plot 3D drawings with his pen plotter. An OpenGL pipeline gives you a raster image. LN gives you 2D vector paths. Every shape is covered in 3D paths. LN chops them into tiny pieces, and from each point shoots a ray toward the camera. If nothing is hit, the point is visible. If something is in the way, it's hidden and never drawn. So the texture is just the paths you choose. Over-eyed paths and a cube become stripes. It also does solid geometry. A sphere trimmed by a cube and drilled by three cylinders. Math functions become surfaces, random walks become strings of beads, and random boxes become a city. Before plotting, there's V-pipe by Antoine Baylor, a Swiss army knife for plotter graphics. creator: mygearhut
caption:
In 1999, id Software open-sourced _Quake III Arena_. Hidden inside was a four-line function calculating the inverse square root 400% faster than CPU silicon hardware, powered by an unexplained hexadecimal constant: `0x5f3759df`.

#programming #math #computerscience #quake3 #algorithms #coding #graphics #vox #gamedev

#quake iii #fast inverse square root #0x5f3759df #computer history #graphics programming #john carmack #algorithms #math explained #software engineering
transcript: In 1999, ID Software open-sourced Quake 3. Buried inside the game engine was a four-line mathematical mystery. It calculated the inverse square root four times faster than silicon hardware, driven by an unexplained hexadecimal number, 0x5F3759DF, and the developer comments simply read, what the fuck. Why was this function so desperate? In 3D graphics, every ray of light, every shadow and every surface reflection requires normalizing vector angles. You divide the vector by its length, one over the square root of x. But on a 1999 Pentium, floating-point division and square root took over 70 clock cycles. Computing millions of them per frame brought CPUs to their knees. The breakthrough started with a bizarre trick. Inside computer memory, a 32-bit floating-point number has a sine, an exponent and a fraction. If you treat those raw bits not as a float, but as an integer, the number behaves logarithmically. Shifting the bits right by one divides the exponent by two. In other words, a simple bit shift calculates a square root. To get the inverse square root, you negate the exponent and subtract the bits from a magic number. That constant had to balance the floating-point exponent bias of 127 and minimize piecewise linear error. When mathematician Greg Walsh calculated the optimal bias, the formula produced 1,597,463,007 0x5F3759DF. The bit-level hack was fast, but it was only an approximation, with about 1% error. To make it game-ready, the code ran a single pass of Newton-Raphson approximation. That single line collapsed the maximum relative error below 0.175%. Suddenly lighting ran at blazing speed, without a single division instruction. For years, programmers thought John Carmack invented it. But investigations traced the ghost back through 3DFX and MATLAB creator Cleve Moeller to Greg Walsh at Ardent Computer in 1988. Today, modern x86 chips have inverse square root baked directly into silicon. But 0x5F3759DF remains the most celebrated hack in computer science history.

DLSS 5 Mod Explosion
#pcgaming #technews #dlss5 #nvidia
transcript: There's been a pretty dramatic explosion of PC gaming mods in the past couple weeks, as if the entire community decided to flip Nvidia the bird and say, don't tell me what I can't do. But whether it's just good old-fashioned contrarian human spirit, or the inevitable result of PC gamers being squeezed from all sides by high prices and imperious future restrictions, is anybody's guess. But just in the past week, DLSS 5 and Frame Generation, which Nvidia says should only work with RTX 50 series GPUs, have been enabled on the RTX 40, 30, and 20 series, first via a redirect that used AMD's FidelityFX FSR solution for FrameGen, and then using Nvidia's native FrameGen via a proxy mod, allowing up to 4x FrameGen with an RTX 3080, and further demoed with an RTX 2060 on Thursday. Modders also addressed DLSS 5's performance impact with an opto-scaler fork that allows DLSS 5 neural rendering to be applied before DLSS super resolution upscaling, resulting in 50% higher frame rates in some tests, a method that has also been added to DLSS 5 Autopilot, which is available on GitHub and allows easier access to multiple community modification tools. This one was tested by Ancient Gameplays, and the performance uplift is significant, without a noticeable drop in visual fidelity. Even long-abandoned dual GPU support is making a comeback to some degree, though calling it SLI wouldn't be accurate. As demonstrated by developer Marcelo Guibo with two RTX 5060 Ti GPUs, DLSS 5 neural rendering can be handled by the second video card as another means of improving performance. Just be careful if you decide to try out these DLSS 5 mods, as they can trigger anti-cheat alarms in some online games, and at least one commenter on Hardforum claims the increased power draw from DLSS 5 testing caused their RTX 5090's connector to melt.
